1.1: 1.1 The words of Ecclesiastes. JEROME on Ecclesiastes, vol. 3. Solomon was called by three names, etc., up to and he is an equal teacher, and does not know that he is king. ALBINUS (Alcuin). The Hebrews relate that this book is of Solomon doing penance, because trusting in wisdom and riches he offended God through women. For he reckoned with himself that all things are vain and that those come to misery who place hope in them. JEROME. Allegorically. The peaceful and beloved Son of God the Father, etc., up to hence: Their sound has gone out into all the earth: and their words to the ends of the world (Psalm 18).
1.2: 1.2 Vanity of vanities. The same. For vanity of vanities, according to certain interpreters, we can say, etc., up to until that which is perfect comes. Before he sets down his sentence, he seems to make a certain preparation and ornament, when he says: Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. Afterward he begins from the greater, that is, from man, showing him subject to vanity, that is to mutability. And this is, vanity, etc. Every living man is vanity: how much more the rest! Hence, The creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of Him who, etc. For whatever can cease to be can be called vanity, because it can be changed. God alone is always the same as what He is. What is changed in a way vanishes, and is not what it was; in comparison with the Creator, every creature can be called vanity and counted as nothing. JEROME. If all things that God made, etc., up to I am compelled to say, not once but twice, Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.
1.3: 1.3 What more has man. The same. After the general sentence, etc., up to but naked they return to the earth from which they were taken.
1.4: 1.4 One generation passes away, etc. The same. The first generation of the Jews departs, etc., up to but we praise God not in one age, but in the ages of ages.
1.5: 1.5 The sun rises and sets. The same. The sun itself, etc., up to which rises to the believer, sets to the unbeliever.
1.6: 1.6 It goes toward the south, etc. The same. From this we can suppose, etc., up to and so returns to the east. The spirit goes round in circuit. The same. He calls the sun itself spirit, etc., up to another would consume the cold.
1.7: 1.7 All the rivers run into the sea. The philosophers say that the sweet waters that flow into the sea are either consumed by the burning sun or are food for the saltness of the sea. But our Ecclesiastes, and the Creator of the waters themselves, says that they return through the hidden veins of the earth to the heads of the springs and from the mother deep always boil up to their own beginnings. By the rivers and the sea we can understand the human race, which returns to the earth from which it was taken, according to that: You are earth, and to earth you shall go (Genesis 3). Nor is the earth filled with the multitude of the dead. And Jerome says torrents, not rivers, because they pass quickly. JEROME. All the torrents, etc., up to as in Proverbs the daughters of the leech.
1.8: 1.8 All things are hard. Man cannot explain the causes and natures of things, nor can the eye look upon them fully, nor the ear, with a teacher instructing, reach the sum of knowledge. For we now see through a mirror in a riddle and in part, until that which is perfect comes (1 Corinthians 13), which cannot be in this mortal body. This sentence is against those who think they have known the holy Scriptures without labor and zeal in speaking, and think themselves wise when they are foolish.
1.9: 1.9 What is that which. JEROME. He seems to speak of these things, etc., up to that God might rest from all His works on the seventh day. What is that which, etc. Of the natures created in the beginning of the world, and of their succession, how they come and pass away; as man dies, man is born, the nature of the one born is the same as that of the one dying. So of birds, fish, serpents and all living things; so of herbs, trees and other natures nothing new is found that was not before: nothing past that will not happen again. Hence, God rested on the seventh day from all His work (Genesis 2), from the creation of new natures, not from governing, according to that: My Father works until now, and I work (John 5). Thus from the primordial seeds of things the time of the whole age is carried through in a natural course.
1.10: 1.10 Nor is it able, etc. JEROME. Is there a word, etc., up to and by the predestination of God those things which are to be have already been made. For it has already gone before. As oblivion hides from us the past things which once were among us, so those who are to be born will not be able to know what is now happening; for they will perish in silence, and will be hidden as though they had not been. For vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, because all things pass like flowing water, and will not return. To this sentence the whole world cries out its assent, and above all the human race.
1.11: 1.11 There is no memory of former things. JEROME. The Seraphim therefore, etc., up to hence afterward, There is no memory of the wise with the fool forever.
1.13: 1.13 And I set my mind, etc. Ecclesiastes therefore set, etc., up to which they incurred of their own will. Thus far generally about the vanities of the world: from here he returns to himself, and shows who he was, how he knew all things, and taught; hence: And I set my mind, etc. This occupation. JEROME. The word anian, which Aquila, the Seventy and Theodotion render in Latin as distension, etc., up to to the higher sense all are referred.
1.14: 1.14 I saw, etc. I considered all worldly things, and saw that it is vanity and malice, that is, afflictions of spirit, by which the mind, wearied with diverse thoughts, labors to know what is not granted to man. JEROME. The word Routh, which Aquila and Theodotion, etc., up to by which the soul is afflicted with diverse thoughts.
1.15: 1.15 The perverse. The same. The perverse cannot be adorned, etc., up to so that it cannot be comprehended.
1.17: 1.17 And errors and fools. The same. The first wisdom is to be free of folly, etc., up to let it suffice to have discussed above.
2.1: 2.1 I said therefore. JEROME. After in the multitude of wisdom, etc., up to then it will not be vanity, but truth.
2.2: 2.2 I counted laughter error. The same. Where we say, etc., up to they promise themselves joyful and prosperous things.
2.3: 2.3 I thought in my heart. The same. Drunkenness, etc., up to what is to be avoided.
2.4: 2.4 I planted vineyards. In the house of the rich man, etc., up to without which the other trees will dry up.
2.6: 2.6 And I built myself pools, etc., up to and awaits the latter rain from heaven.
2.7: 2.7 I possessed servants: serving through fear, and desiring spiritual things, and not fearing. We call those home-born who are indeed of the Church, and precede the aforesaid servants and handmaids; yet they are not free. Home-born are called the sons of servants, born in the house of their master. And herds, and great ones. These are those who without reason and knowledge of the Scriptures labor indeed in the Church, but have not yet reached the man, that is, the image of God. JEROME. And indeed the possession of herds. Note that, etc., up to or the home-born.
2.8: 2.8 The substances of kings. The same. The doctrines of the philosophers, etc., up to and he rejects the prudence of the prudent. I made for myself singers. A singer, etc., up to, Singers, men and women, both sexes delighted me. The delights of the sons of men. Wisdom, namely, which, like paradise, has various fruits and manifold pleasures. Of which the Psalmist: Delight in the Lord, and He will give you the requests of your heart (Psalm 36). And, You shall give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure (Psalm 35).
2.9: 2.9 Who were before me in Jerusalem. Literally: It is not great praise. For before Solomon reigned Saul, in whose time the kingdom began, and David, under whom the kingdom was quite small. It persevered. Others: stood, that is, wisdom remained with him placed in the flesh, not advancing by moments, as in us, but standing in fullness.
2.10: 2.10 And all things that. But the more zeal with which these things grew, the more wisdom was lacking, because it carried me off through all desires, and I thought this to be the fruit of my labors, if I served lust; but at last, returning to myself, I saw that all were vain.
2.11: 2.11 Under the sun. JEROME. In Christ. In the sun He has set His tabernacle. He therefore who has not yet attained to the order and constancy of the brightness of the sun, in him Christ does not dwell.
2.13: 2.13 And I saw that so much. When I was thinking this, that the wise man is light, the fool darkness: the eyes of the one in heaven, of the other on earth, there suddenly crept upon me why they perish by a common death, are pressed down by a common misery, and the like.
2.18: 2.18 Again I detested. JEROME. By spiritual labor the saints meditate day and night in the law of the Lord, etc., up to for it is not wisdom to gather earthly riches. About to have. This happened to Solomon himself, who had a son not like himself, Rehoboam. From which we understand that a son, if he is foolish, is not even worthy of his father's inheritance.
2.21: 2.21 For when another. The same. Above of the uncertain heir, etc., up to from reason.
2.24: 2.24 Is it not better. The same. After I have handled all things, etc., up to as much as suffices?
2.26: 2.26 To a good man. The same. To one amending his ways, etc., up to and to be composed by the presumption of the spirit.
3.1: 3.1 All things have their time. JEROME. Above he taught the uncertain and fluctuating state of the human condition, etc., up to they are contained neither in place nor in time.
3.2: 3.2 A time to plant, etc. The same. It is doubtful to no one, etc., up to because perfect charity casts out fear.
3.3: 3.3 A time to destroy, etc. We cannot build good things unless we first destroy evil ones, as was said to Jeremiah by God, that he first uproot and dig under and destroy, and afterward build and plant (Jeremiah 1).
3.4: 3.4 A time to mourn, etc. We must mourn now that in the future we may dance, that dance which David danced before the ark of the covenant (2 Kings 6). Displeasing the daughter of Saul, he pleased God the more.
3.5: 3.5 A time to scatter stones, etc. JEROME. I wonder, etc., up to and calls to penance. A time to embrace. A time to embrace wisdom and to cling more closely to contemplation; and a time to be far from the embrace, namely of wisdom, that we may serve the cares of the time, and those things without which we cannot live.
3.7: 3.7 A time to be silent and a time. JEROME. We teach in the churches what we do not know. We do not learn all arts without a teacher; only this one is so cheap and so easy that it needs no instructor. Nothing seems right to us except what we learn, so that after much silence we become teachers from disciples. A time to speak. The discipline of Pythagoras is to be silent for five years, and afterward the learned speak.
3.8: 3.8 A time of love. A time to love, after God, wives, children, relatives, and a time to hate them, in martyrdom. Or, since now we see through a mirror in a riddle (1 Corinthians 13), etc. There will be a time to love the presence of God, and a time to hate, when, seeing face to face, and advancing to better, we shall begin to hate and despise what we loved. A time of war. Now, for those not doing penance; a time of peace in the future, when all Israel shall be saved; A time of war, that you not be secure, take the armor of God.
3.10: 3.10 I have seen the affliction which He has given, etc. JEROME. It is said that for this reason God, etc., up to up to the end of the age He made to grow, remain and change.
3.12: 3.12 And I knew. JEROME. Therefore man was given as a husbandman in the world, etc., up to hence:
3.13: 3.13 Every man who eats and drinks, etc. For many now are the tribulations of the just, but in the future there will be no labor in Jacob. I have learned, etc. The same. There is nothing new in the world, the course of the sun, the changes of the moon, the dryness or greenness of earth and trees, were established with the world; and God tempered these by a fixed reason, that in them we may understand the Providence of God, and fear before the face of God. And the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil.
3.16: 3.16 I saw under the sun. The same. When in this world I sought judgment and truth, etc., up to, For all things will be required in their time.
3.17: 3.17 I said in my heart. The same. As if, etc., up to and the earth to be filled with cattle and herds.
3.21: 3.21 Who knows. The same. He does not say, etc., up to and be a sure asserter of a matter as if doubtful. Downward. To the underworld. For it can happen that they are quickly changed, and often those who seemed learned are led down to the underworld; and simple rustics are crowned.
3.22: 3.22 And I perceived. Troubled by the former error, etc., up to what will be in the world afterward.
4.1: 4.1 I turned myself to other things. David in Psalm 72, and Jeremiah in his volume, treat this place more fully.
4.2: 4.2 And I praised. JEROME. Others understand this place thus, etc., up to and that they are blessed as long as they enjoy the angelic choir.
4.3: 4.3 And happier. Because he neither saw these evils nor experienced them: nor according to the error of those who think souls exist before men are made. It is therefore better not to be at all than to live badly: hence, It were better for him if that man had not been born, etc. (Matthew 14).
4.9: 4.9 It is better. The same. After the anxieties and miseries, etc., up to we are not able to receive the warmth of eternal life.
4.13: 4.13 Better is a child. The same, up to the end of the chapter.
5.1: 5.1 Not rashly, God. Because He hears and sees all things, and convicts your folly, though He is in heaven and you on earth.
5.2: 5.2 Many. As one who thinks of many things frequently dreams of them, so he falls into folly who disputes about God beyond himself. Or, because now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, as through a dream, we suppose we hold what we do not have, and yet have nothing.
5.3: 5.3 When you have made a vow. JEROME. It is better not to promise, etc., up to, he shall be beaten with many stripes.
5.4: 5.4 And much. As the Jews who said: All that the Lord has commanded us we will do (Exodus 24, 32): and they adored the calf.
5.5: 5.5 Do not give your mouth. As if: do not say that you sin from the weakness of your flesh, as though throwing the blame back on the author. Before the angel. Who stands by each one and reports everything to God: do not think that anything is hidden from God.
5.6: 5.6 Where there are many. As if: Do not give your mouth, etc., because this life is like dreams, and many things seem true that are false; so also your excuse.
5.7: 5.7 If you see oppressions. As if he said: Do not say before the angel, there is no Providence: which is against those who think all things are done by chance, and deny the providence of God. But if you see the oppressions of the needy, etc.
5.8: 5.8 Of all the earth, etc. God is patient and a repayer, who says, When I shall take a time, I will judge justices.
5.11: 5.11 Sweet is the sleep. JEROME. The rich miser, etc., up to since they themselves will see God.
5.12: 5.12 There is also another infirmity. We can say these things of the philosophers, etc., up to when it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, etc.
5.17: 5.17 This therefore seemed good to me, etc. He says it is better, etc., up to which the grace of God inspires in helping good works.
6.1: 6.1 There is also another evil. He describes also in another way the rich miser, who although he has all good things, nevertheless torments himself with excessive thrift, not knowing for whom he gathers.
6.2: 6.2 A man to whom God has given riches. JEROME. This can be taken of the people of Israel, etc., up to to judgment we all hasten.
6.3: 6.3 Burial. The same. So avaricious that he does not even think of burial, or, often killed for his riches he is cast out unburied: or, because he leaves no memory of himself, though he abounds in all goods.
6.7: 6.7 All the labor: that is, what man, that is the rational one, has learned by laboring, he has in his mouth, because he teaches others. His soul shall not be filled. The same. Because he always desires to learn what he may teach: and he has this more than the fool, because with the blessed poor man he tends to Christ, who is the life and who says: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
6.10: 6.10 He who is to be. The same. God already knows the name of all men who are to be clothed with a body; lest man be able to answer back against the craftsman, why he was made thus or thus. For the more we inquire, the more our vanity and superfluous words are shown; and free will is not taken away by the foreknowledge of God, but causes precede why each thing was made.
6.11: 6.11 The words are. As if: man will indeed be the son of God, but do not inquire further what kind, how and of what sort, but believe his generation.
7.2: 7.2 A good name is better. JEROME. The memory of good works, which delights the hearts of hearers, as ointments the nostrils: Hence, The memory of the just is in praise, the name of the wicked shall rot. And the day. That is, it is better to escape by dying the torments and tribulations and labors of a miserable life, than to be born to these and endure them.
7.4: 7.4 Better is anger, against one's own sin or another's, because you correct, not because you desire revenge (Proverbs 27).
7.6: 7.6 It is better to be rebuked by a wise man. Better are the wounds of a friend than the deceitful kisses of an enemy. The words of a flatterer are more senseless, moving to thorns, that is, the cares of the world, which lead to the fires of Gehenna: the perfect wise man needs no cleverness, is troubled by no calumny. Therefore it is to be taken of the wise man who is in progress, who is sometimes troubled at the iniquity of judgment, when God does not punish at once.
7.9: 7.9 Better is the end. Perfection. He who perseveres shall be saved. Better is justice completed than begun, and the end of prayer than its beginnings; here the contest, there the victory. The arrogant. Opposite to this arrogant one is he who in the Gospel is read as poor in spirit (Matthew 5).
7.11: 7.11 What do you think? Otherwise: you ought so to live that the present days are always better for you than the past. For there is always time for working, lest when you begin to decline it be said: You ran well, who hindered you from obeying the truth? (Galatians 5).
7.14: 7.14 Consider the works of God. How great, how wonderful; one He chose by free kindness, another He despises by just judgment, hence, Jacob I loved, Esau I hated (Malachi 1). And, All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.
7.15: 7.15 The evil day. JEROME. Of judgment, which seems evil to the evil, hence, That day, a day of wrath, etc. Or, endure good and evil, that is prosperity and adversity, manfully, as they justly come. For all things are just, though hidden, and this is let him not find, etc.
7.18: 7.18 And be not. The wicked shall not live out half their days; as if: Do not, impenitent, provoke God to inflict punishment on you even while living, as He did to Dathan and Abiram.
7.19: 7.19 He neglects nothing. He does good to all without respect of persons. Or, He provides in prosperity and in adversity.
7.20: 7.20 Ten princes. JEROME. The angels, who preside over our city, that is the Church, as guardians, that is helpers. And they are called ten, because ten is a perfect number.
7.22: 7.22 But also all. He teaches the wise man not to heed the tongues of slanderers, lest, doing the same himself, he wish to be pardoned and others reproved. For if he does this, he will always be curious and angry, because he will not be able to restrain even the tongues of servants.
7.27: 7.27 Of hunters, of demons, who hunt our souls, whose women are the nets, and the dragnets heretics.
7.28: 7.28 Behold this. This I found, etc., up to the woman is easier to fall. That I might find the reason. Any matter or distinction between men and their ways: who is perfectly good but Christ alone?
7.29: 7.29 A man. Christ, who is the head of all good things, which is figured by the thousand, a perfect number.
7.30: 7.30 Only this. JEROME. Lest he seem to condemn the common nature of all men and accuse God its author, he watchfully added, Only, etc. As if he said: Man was indeed made good, but left to free will, he falls of his own accord and mixes himself with vain and superfluous cares. Who is such as the wise man, etc. The same. He said above that a good man is hardly found, although men were made good by God. Now he enumerates as if rejoicing what good things He gave them: wisdom, reason, to know hidden things.
8.2: 8.2 I keep the king's mouth. JEROME. He seems indeed to command, according to the Apostle, etc., up to his will is to be obeyed.
8.4: 8.4 Nor can anyone say to him, etc. The same. The commands of God are not to be discussed as to why He commanded them, but done.
8.8: 8.8 It is not in man's power. The same. As if: you ought not to take it ill if you cannot know the future, if you are often oppressed by more powerful wicked men, because all things quickly end, and death snatches all equally.
8.10: 8.10 I saw the wicked buried, etc. They do not repent even in death, whose accusation, the rarer and harder it is, the greater seems to them the freedom of sinning.
8.14: 8.14 There are just men to whom evils come, etc. As to the sons of Aaron sacrificing, according to the Hebrew, and Manasseh, who after so many evils was brought back from captivity to the kingdom and lived happily.
9.1: 9.1 There are just men, etc. A dog is better. JEROME. The living dog is the poor just man, the dead lion the powerful unjust man, who carries nothing with him out of the world.
9.5: 9.5 But the dead. The same. Some assert that even after death they grow, etc., up to rational creatures and to merit.
9.10: 9.10 They will be. That is, they will avail you after death.
9.11: 9.11 War. Of the victors or even imitators of war, according to that: Without me you can do nothing. Riches. Of good works.
9.12: 9.12 As fish are taken. Heretics also have their net cast, and snares with which they catch the simple.
9.15: 9.15 A poor man. Christ, of whom the Psalm: I am poor and sorrowful (Psalm 68). And in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2). By his wisdom. Not by power.
9.17: 9.17 The words of the wise. JEROME. Who do not seek favor and applause, but the salvation of the hearers: nor cry out to be heard, but desire to be heard favorably. Among fools. Fools who do not seek to profit, but to win praise for themselves.
10.4: 10.4 Place. Hold the station of faith, lest you be overcome: and do not carry out if you have already thought ill. He who digs. He opened a pit, and dug it out: and falls into the pit he made.
10.11: 10.11 If it bite. JEROME. As if: as a serpent biting secretly pours in venom, so does he who detracts. Or, the serpent, that is the devil, bites in silence, when he who has sinned at the devil's persuasion is unwilling to confess.
10.19: 10.19 In laughter they make bread and wine, that those drinking may feast. They preach more to allure than to profit. All things obey money, etc. And the priests taught for a reward.
10.20: 10.20 In your thought, etc. He simply warns that we not curse our superiors either in anger or lightness, because what we said is often reported to them, even when we did not fear it, even if it was in the bedchamber.
11.1: 11.1 Send your bread. Fit for bearing fruit.
11.2: 11.2 Give portions to seven. JEROME. The Old Testament, whose seventh day, that is the sabbath, is specially honored; and also to eight, which is the New; for without the one the other does not avail.
11.3: 11.3 If the tree fall to the south or to the north, the same: as if he said: The place that you prepare for yourself here, you will have in the future.
11.4: 11.4 He who observes the wind does not sow. The same. As if he said: Give yourself to the Almighty, either bodily comfort or the word of God, lest perhaps you pass by one who is worthy to receive; and at every time. He who observes the wind. One must sow in the midst of the storm, because we do not know what the will of the spirit is, and this is, How, etc.
11.6: 11.6 In the morning sow your seed, etc. The same. At every time, from morning to evening, and conversely: or in boyhood and in old age. For he who perseveres will be saved.
11.9: 11.9 Rejoice therefore, young man, etc. The same. From here to the end of the book, etc., up to let them know they are to be judged.
12.1: 12.1 From here to the end of the chapter it is read in three ways, namely of judgment, old age, captivity, and some glosses serve sometimes two senses, sometimes are found according to all the senses.
12.2: 12.2 Before the sun and the light, and the stars and the moon are darkened, etc. JEROME. The sun shall be turned into darkness, etc., up to the clouds and rains cease for it.
12.4: 12.4 And they shall shut the doors in the street, that they may not see the sports of the young: for all such things are unbearable to them. And they shall rise up. Because they cannot sleep, the blood growing cold, the humor by which sleep is nourished being dried up.
12.5: 12.5 The caper-berry shall be scattered. JEROME. The caper is good for the kidneys, etc., up to in adversity they desist from the good.
12.6: 12.6 Before the silver cord is broken. He returns to the higher things, where he says: Remember your Creator, etc., he concludes the sentence with a similar end.
12.7: 12.7 And let it return. Before you return to Babylon, from which you went out in the loins of Abraham, and begin to be worn down in Mesopotamia, from which you set out.
12.8: 12.8 Vanity of vanities. After the description of human frailty and death, he beautifully concludes what he had proposed: Vanity of vanities. As if: do not run riot, do not seek delights, since you know that you pass away with a swift end and hasten to judgment.
12.11: 12.11 The words of the wise. JEROME. Lest he seem rashly to forge new precepts after the law given through Moses, God Himself forewarning, he says these are the words of the wise.
12.13: 12.13 The end of speaking. Because, like a preacher, he had brought in the diverse opinions of diverse people: with this end he reconciles all, namely, Fear God. The Hebrews say that this alone is held to be of authority, because here he shows his intention, whereas in many places he seems to exhort to pleasures.
